extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and applicants drafting or prosecuting AI/ML-related patent applications (esp. before the USPTO and other major offices)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and prosecuting patent applications for AI/machine learning inventions to satisfy eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101), written description/enablement/claim support (35 U.S.C. §112), and inventorship requirements across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical idea embodied in a computer (patent eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technical idea embodied within a 'general purpose computer' may be sufficient to satisfy patent eligibility if software and hardware operate together; inventions that are purely economic laws, mathematical formulas, mental activity, etc., may fail patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure software claims show software+hardware interaction or otherwise demonstrate a concrete technical idea beyond abstract ideas; avoid claiming mere abstract concepts (economic laws, mathematical formulas, mental activity) without technical implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Korea enablement: input/output relationship for trained models
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement in Korea may require the application include a description of a relationship (e.g., a correlation) between input data and output data from a trained model to implement AI-related inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe learning data, correlations between learning data and solutions to the technical problem, the learning model/method based on input data, and how a trained model is generated from input data and methods to demonstrate enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japan enablement/support: capacity to create learned model with certain accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be clear and sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to work the invention; for AI, the specification should state that the invention can achieve a certain degree of accuracy in estimation processing and, if there is any relationship between input and output data in training data, describe that relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include disclosure that the AI can create a learned model achieving required accuracy and detail the input-output relationships used in training; failure to disclose correlations between different feature values and outputs can cause failure of support/enablement (e.g., JPO Case Example 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: China: consider claims as a whole (Section 9.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For AI/big data applications, technical features, algorithms, business rules, and process steps should not be evaluated separately; the claim as a whole should be considered when assessing patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and specifications to show how all recited features work together; avoid relying on isolated analysis of algorithmic or business-rule elements divorced from their technical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: China inventive-step guidance for algorithmic adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim limitations differ from existing technology in terms of algorithm adjustments that solve a technical problem, the claims may possess an inventive step (e.g., adjusting a CNN to process variable image sizes to achieve a technical effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize algorithmic changes that achieve a technical effect or solve a technical problem rather than mere abstract or business-method improvements; provide examples and technical rationale tying algorithmic differences to technical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: China written description: interaction of technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should clearly provide how technical features support and interact with each other in their functionality to solve a technical problem; include at least one input parameter and at least one output related to the specific technology area for algorithms, and detailed explanations for business rules/method features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how features interact to produce technical effects; if user-experience improvements are objective, specify how they are implemented via technical features and how features interact to generate those effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship: natural person requirement and practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jurisdictions require inventors to be natural persons; AI/non-human inventors generally cannot be named in the USA, UK, EPO, JPO, Switzerland, Korea, China, etc., leading to practical issues (oath/declaration, assignment, ownership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name human contributors who conceived claimed subject matter; identify aspects traceable to human conception; consider keeping AI-generated aspects as trade secrets or excluding them from claims if conception cannot be traced to a human; monitor litigation and jurisdictional developments where AI has been named as inventor (e.g., South Africa, Australia, certain PCT filings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-part test application for AI (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Alice/Mayo test: (1) determine if claims fall into statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition); (2A prong 1) ask whether the claims recite an abstract idea; (2A prong 2) consider if the claim is integrated into a practical application; (2B) determine whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing eligibility for AI inventions, address each prong explicitly—show statutory category, explain why the claim is not an abstract idea or is integrated into a practical application, and identify additional elements (improvements, particular machines, transformations, unconventional steps) that amount to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid functional claiming (risk under §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims described using functional language or broad 'black box' functional limitations have been held ineligible even with concrete elements (e.g., American Axle, Yu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claims that merely recite high-level functionality without structure; include structural/architectural detail or specific steps to tie claimed functions to concrete implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim AI-specific architecture or training elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting AI-specific architecture (e.g., CNN, RNN) or training elements can support patent eligibility because such elements are not 'generic computing environments' and can be integrated into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim particular machine components (convolutional neural network, recurrent neural network, specific training stages/processes) and training processes to show non-conventionality; include architectural details in claims and specification where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on training-process claims (MPEP Example 39)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting a method of training a neural network (specific staged training, datasets, transformations) are recognized in MPEP Example 39 as not reciting an abstract idea and can be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft training claims with concrete staged processes, data transformations, and dataset construction details to align with MPEP examples and reduce §101 risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/solution claim style to show technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can avoid §101 rejections by reciting (1) a problem to be overcome, (2) a technical solution (often ML steps), and (3) the resulting improvement over prior art or improvement to computer/AI functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure claims and specification to explicitly identify the problem, the technical steps/solution, and the measurable or concrete result; use problem/solution examples (e.g., converting non-standardized information to standardized format, generating a depth map to avoid obstacles) to demonstrate improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of AI-specific improvements to claim and describe
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of AI-specific improvements that support eligibility include improving predicted annotation accuracy, reducing size or layers of networks, improving inference accuracy, reducing required training data, enabling different kinds of training data, improving training speed/efficiency, enabling lifelong learning, reducing parameters, increasing speed/efficiency of operation/prediction, enabling hardware optimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, claim and demonstrate one or more concrete AI-specific improvements in the specification and claims, and provide data/analysis showing the improvement relative to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art unit selection and classification strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because treatment of AI applications varies across USPTO art units, drafting to direct an application to an art unit more favorable to subject-matter eligibility (e.g., image processing/Class 382) can improve chances of allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a title, claim preambles, and claim emphasis that clearly identify the technical field (e.g., image processing) and include independent claim language that aligns with the target art unit's subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid black-box descriptions to satisfy §112
rubrics_metrics.description: AI/ML inventions should not be described as a black box; include details related to architecture, training, and problem/solution to satisfy written description and enablement requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple levels of description (architectural, training, functional) and concrete algorithmic descriptions where applicable; avoid merely asserting that an AI/system 'does' something without structural or procedural detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture description: three levels of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe AI architecture at three levels: (1) functional component (e.g., image classification neural network), (2) high-level architectural paradigm (CNN, RNN, feed-forward), and (3) technical details at layer/node/activation-function level (without needing to disclose every internal parameter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate the problem to the chosen architecture, explain how the architecture performs claimed functions, and, where possible, weave the inventive concept into each abstraction level to meet §112 support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training description: three levels of abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe training at three levels: (1) functional description of the trained network's purpose, (2) high-level training paradigm (supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement), and (3) fine details such as loss functions or policy models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough training detail to show how the trained model is generated and why it performs the claimed functions—this supports enablement without necessarily disclosing exact parameter values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/solution disclosure requirements for §112
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a description of the technical problem, a description of the structure that performs each claimed function (including algorithms if software/AI), non-limiting definitions for AI-specific terms, and how the solution results in an improvement over existing systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the field, give a generic device/task name, explain the problem without conceding unnecessary background, and clearly tie the structure/algorithm to the claimed improvement; ensure specification supports the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting to withstand CAFC/PTAB challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive judicial review, claims and specifications should show concrete technical improvements and AI-specific elements/architecture; courts have denied early dismissal where plausible technical improvements are pled (e.g., LPHDR architecture improving computer performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize technical improvements in the specification and claims, provide factual/technical support for inventive effects, and avoid overly broad claims that risk preemption; use PTAB and district court examples (e.g., Ex parte Hannun, Singular Computing, Applied Predictive Techs.) to guide claim/pleading strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specification examples and data to show improvement (PTAB Hannun lesson)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB stressed the importance of the specification describing how a claimed invention provides an improvement to the technical field (e.g., demonstrating higher performance of a trained neural network versus traditional methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include comparative statements, performance data, or concrete technical explanations in the specification demonstrating why the claimed approach improves the technical field to aid both examiner and judicial analyses.
